title: Hymns to the Sun and to Athena
source_text: Εἶτα πάλιν ὁ Κέλσος ὁμοίως τοῖς ἀπὸ δαιμονισμοῦ ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε ἀναφέρουσιν εἶτα πάλιν καταπίπτουσιν ὥσπερ νήφων τοιαῦτά τινα λέγων· ἐὰν μέντοι γε κελεύῃ τις, εἰ τύχοι θρησκεύων θεὸν, ἢ ἀσεβεῖν ἢ ἄλλο τι αἰσχρὸν εἰπεῖν, οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς πιστευτέον ἀλλὰ πρὸ τούτων πάσας βασάνους ἐγκαρτερητέον καὶ πάντας θανάτους ὑπομενετέον, πρίν τι ἀνόσιον περὶ θεοῦ μὴ ὅτι γε εἰπεῖν ἀλλὰ μελῆσαι· εἶτα πάλιν ἀπ᾿ ἀγνοίας τῆς περὶ τοῦ ἡμετέρου λόγου καὶ πρὸς ταύτῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ φύρειν τὰ πάντα τοιαῦτά φησιν· ἐὰν δὲ κελεύῃ τις εὐφημῆσαι τὸν Ἥλιον ἢ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν προθυμότατα μετὰ καλοῦ παιᾶνος εὐφημεῖν, οὕτω τοι σέβειν μᾶλλον δόξεις τὸν μέγαν θεὸν, ἐὰν καὶ τούσδε ὑμνῇς· τὸ γὰρ θεοσεβὲς διὰ πάντων διεξιὸν τελεώτερον γίνεται. φαμὲν οὖν ὅτι οὐ περιμένομεν εὐφημῆσαι τὸν Ἥλιον τὸν κελεύοντα, οἱ μαθόντες οὐ μόνον τοὺς τῇ διατάξει ὑποτεταγμένους εὐφημεῖν ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς. εὐφημοῦμεν οὖν Ἥλιον ὡς καλὸν θεοῦ δημιούργημα καὶ τοὺς νόμους φυλάσσον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἀκοῦον τοῦ „αἰνεῖτε τὸν κύριον ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη,“ καὶ ὅση δύναμις ὑμνοῦντα τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὸν δημιουργὸν τοῦ παντός. Ἀθηνᾶν μέντοι μετὰ Ἡλίου τασσομένην ἐμυθοποίησαν οἱ Ἑλλήνων λόγοι, εἴτ᾿ ἐν ὑπονοίαις εἴτε χωρὶς ὑπονοιῶν φάσκοντες ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Διὸς γεγεννῆσθαι κεφαλῆς καθωπλισμένην· καὶ διωκομένην τότε ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἡφαίστου. βουλομένου αὐτῆς φθεῖραι τὴν παρθενίαν, ἐκπεφευγέναι μὲν αὐτὸν τὴν δ᾿ ἐκ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας πεσοῦσαν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν θορὴν ἀγαπήσασαν ἐκθρέψαι, καλέσασαν Ἐριχθόνιον, τόν ποτε, φασὶν, Ἀθήνη θρέψε, Διὸς θυγάτηρ, τέκε δὲ ζείδωρος ἄρουρα. καὶ ὁρῶμέν γε ὅτι τῷ προσιεμένῳ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν, Διὸς θυγατέρα, πολλοὺς μύθους καὶ πλάσματα παρεκδεκτέον, οὓς οὐκ ἂν παραδέχοιτο ὁ φεύγων μὲν μύθους ζητῶν δὲ ἀλήθειαν.
pass_a_gloss: Then again Celsus, like those who from demonic possession (δαιμονισμός) sometimes come back up (ἀναφέρω) and then again fall down (καταπίπτω), as though sober (νήφω), saying some such things: 'If, however, someone commands (κελεύω) one who happens to be worshipping (θρησκεύω) God either to be impious (ἀσεβέω) or to say something else shameful (αἰσχρός), in no way at all (οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς) must he be trusted/heeded (πιστευτέον); but before these things all tortures (βάσανος) must be endured (ἐγκαρτερητέον) and all deaths undergone (ὑπομενετέον), before one, not to say speak, but even think/care (μελῆσαι) anything unholy (ἀνόσιος) about God.' Then again from ignorance (ἄγνοια) of our doctrine (λόγος), and in addition from confusing (φύρω) all things, he says such things: 'But if someone commands (you) to speak well of / praise (εὐφημέω) Helios (the Sun) or Athena, most eagerly (προθυμότατα) with a fine paean (παιάν) to praise them; thus indeed you will seem to revere (σέβω) the great God more, if you also hymn (ὑμνέω) these; for piety toward God (τὸ θεοσεβές) going through (διεξιόν) all things becomes more complete (τελεώτερον).' We say, then, that we do not wait for (περιμένω) the one commanding (in order) to praise Helios, we who have learned to speak well of not only those ranked under the ordering (διάταξις, ὑποτάσσω) but also enemies (ἐχθρός). We praise, then, Helios as a fine handiwork (δημιούργημα) of God, both keeping (φυλάσσω) the laws of God and hearing (ἀκούω) the 'Praise (αἰνέω) the Lord, sun and moon', and with all its power hymning the Father and Creator/Craftsman (δημιουργός) of the all. Athena, however, ranked with (τάσσω μετά) Helios, the accounts (λόγοι) of the Greeks made into myth (μυθοποιέω), saying, whether in hidden meanings (ὑπόνοια) or without hidden meanings, that she was born (γεννάω) armed (καθοπλίζω) from the head of Zeus; and that, pursued (διώκω) then by Hephaestus wishing to destroy (φθείρω) her virginity (παρθενία), she escaped him, but loved and reared (ἐκτρέφω) the seed (θορή) fallen from the desire (ἐπιθυμία) onto the earth, calling it Erichthonius, 'whom once,' they say, 'Athena reared, daughter of Zeus, and the grain-giving (ζείδωρος) earth/ploughland (ἄρουρα) bore (τίκτω).' And we see that one admitting (προσίεμαι) Athena, daughter of Zeus, must accept besides (παρεκδέχομαι) many myths and fabrications (πλάσμα), which one fleeing myths and seeking truth would not accept.
pass_b_english: Then again Celsus, like those who at times recover from demonic possession and then fall back again, says something like this, as though he were sober: “If, however, someone should command one who happens to worship God either to act impiously or to say anything else shameful, he must in no way at all be obeyed; rather than this, one must endure every torture and submit to every kind of death, before one would even think, let alone say, anything unholy about God.” Then again, out of ignorance of our teaching, and besides that because he jumbles everything together, he says this: “But if someone commands you to praise the Sun or Athena, praise them with the utmost eagerness in a fine hymn; in this way you will seem all the more to worship the great God, if you hymn these too; for piety becomes more complete when it passes through all things.”

We answer, then, that we do not wait for someone to command us before we praise the sun, we who have learned to speak well not only of those who are subject to God’s ordering but even of our enemies (compare Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28). So we praise the sun as a fine work of God, which keeps the laws of God and hears the words, “Praise the Lord, sun and moon” (Psalm 148:3), and which with all its power hymns the Father and Creator of the universe.

As for Athena, however, whom the accounts of the Greeks set beside the sun, they made her the subject of myth, saying, whether with hidden meanings or without them, that she was born fully armed from the head of Zeus; and that once, when Hephaestus pursued her in the wish to destroy her virginity, she escaped him, but that she loved the seed which fell to the earth from his lust and reared it, calling it Erichthonius, “whom once,” they say, “Athena, daughter of Zeus, reared, but the grain-giving earth bore” (Homer, Iliad 2.547–548). And we see that one who accepts Athena, the daughter of Zeus, must accept with her many myths and fictions, which one who flees from myths and seeks the truth would not accept.

choices.choice: Ἥλιος is the same word for the sun-god and the sun: rendered ‘the Sun’ (capitalised) in Celsus’s words, where it is a deity to be hymned, and ‘the sun’ in Origen’s reply, where he treats it as a created body. Psalm 148:3 is the same number in the Septuagint and English Bibles. The phrase ‘speak well of ... even our enemies’ is an allusion to the command to bless those who curse and to love enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28; compare Romans 12:14); εὐφημεῖν keeps the play on Celsus’s word ‘praise’. ‘Those who are subject to God’s ordering’ renders τοὺς τῇ διατάξει ὑποτεταγμένους (literally ‘those ranked under the ordering’); ‘God’s’ is supplied from context. πιστευτέον literally ‘must be trusted’; here ‘obeyed/heeded’. In ‘κελεύῃ τις, εἰ τύχοι θρησκεύων θεόν’ the participle is nominative and so grammatically goes with τις (the one who commands); Celsus’s Greek is loose here, and the rendering follows the sense the sentence needs (the worshipper is the one commanded); the main point, that a command to impiety must never be obeyed, stands on either reading. In Celsus’s second sentence the second infinitive (εὐφημεῖν) is the main clause (‘praise them’), and προθυμότατα with a fine paean goes with both the Sun and Athena. The Homer lines (Iliad 2.547-548) are said there of Erechtheus; the myth applies them to Erichthonius, as Origen’s source does. ‘with a fine paean’ rendered ‘in a fine hymn’.
'come round for a time' -> 'at times recover' (ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε = sometimes)
Celsus's second quotation restructured: 'praise the Sun or Athena, praise them with the utmost eagerness' (second εὐφημεῖν is the apodosis; eagerness was wrongly tied to Athena alone)
Homer quotation put in natural English order ('Athena, daughter of Zeus, reared')
note added on the nominative θρησκεύων (grammar points to the commander; sense rendering kept)
Psalm 148:3 (LXX = English number), Iliad 2.547-548 checked: correct

choices.choice: 8.66: In 'κελεύῃ τις, εἰ τύχοι θρησκεύων θεόν' the participle is nominative, so the grammar points to the one giving the command. The translation keeps the sense reading, that the worshipper is the one commanded. The ambiguity is recorded in translator_notes. The main point is the same on either reading: a command to impiety must never be obeyed. Passed.
